## How this project came to be

```{=html}
{{< include images/_timeline.svg >}}
```

::: {.small-note}
33 discussion docs · 6 experiments and 7 tools developed to answer discussion questions
:::

::: {.notes}
October 2024: the first version, zombie_radio_ai, made by hand in a couple of days for a hackathon, no AI assistant —
they were not good enough then. Many of the show's ideas come from it. Then TalkWithMe, the app we built on (its first
version written by an AI, Qwen), and four weeks of zombie-radio: the docs first, then the fork, and a release every
day or two. The numbers were counted on 2026-10-03 (recount before the talk); the 7 tools: fetch EARS, screen the
voices, cast the voices, fetch from Freesound, prepare the static bed, drive a show, replay a voice chunk.
:::

## A Halloween broadcast {.smaller .boxed-columns}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### October 30, 1938

The eve of Halloween. Orson Welles and the Mercury Theatre on the Air broadcast *The War of the Worlds* on CBS radio:
a Martian invasion, told as breaking news.

![](images/war-of-the-worlds-1938.jpg){.col-img fig-alt="Orson Welles at the CBS microphone, and a 1938 editorial cartoon: Help! Men from Mars!"}

::: {.credit .centered}
Wikimedia Commons, public domain
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### October 2026

Zombie-Radio borrows the frame: an emergency broadcast already in progress, scientists trapped in a lab, a failing
shortwave radio — that sometimes listens.

![](images/old-radio-look.jpg){.col-img fig-alt="The show's old-radio look: a 1950 Philips Sirius radio with the transcript on its speaker cloth"}

::: {.credit .centered}
Radio photo: Bin im Garten, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The bridge from the clip to the show. Set the atmosphere: fun and fake horror.
:::

## About this project

::: {.about-block .about-code}
[Our code: Two open repositories (MIT)]{.about-head}

::: {.about-row}
::: {.about-card}
**github.com/alfre2v/TalkWithZombies** — the app: a fork of TalkWithMe adding the show engine (Python director,
grammar, streaming voice, listener's turn) and an old-radio stage
:::
::: {.about-card}
**github.com/alfre2v/zombie-radio** — the infrastructure and the record: Ansible and Docker for the model servers and
the laptop, the voice tools, the specs and design discussions
:::
:::
:::

::: {.about-row}
::: {.about-block .about-principles}
[Two principles]{.about-head}

1. **Local AI first, cloud-capable**: every model open and self-hosted; the same deploy to a home GPU or a rented one
2. **Live improvisation**: the drama is improvised at broadcast time, not scripted
:::
::: {.about-block .about-goals}
[Four goals]{.about-head}

1. Story coherence and improvisation
2. Emotional voices, in sync with the story
3. One-command deploy to a cloud GPU
4. Same deploy, for local GPU
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The owner's full wording.

The code — two open repositories (MIT License):

github.com/alfre2v/TalkWithZombies — the app: a fork of the open-source TalkWithMe that adds the show engine (the
Python director, the grammar, the streaming voice, the listener's turn) and the browser stage, styled as an old radio
set.

github.com/alfre2v/zombie-radio — the infrastructure and the record: Ansible and Docker playbooks that stand up the
three model servers on a GPU and install the app on a laptop, the tools that cast the voices, and the specs and design
discussions from the whole build.

Two principles: 1. Local AI first, cloud-capable — every show-time model (dialogue LLM, text-to-speech, speech
recognition) is open and self-hosted; the backend deploys identically to a home Linux GPU box or a rented cloud GPU
instance. 2. Theatrical live improvisation with LLMs — the drama is improvised at broadcast time, not scripted.

Goals: 1. Story coherence and improvisation — the LLM improvises a credible human interaction. 2. Emotional voices
support narration — real voices with emotion, in sync with story. 3. Automated deployment to cloud GPU — easy install
AI components to a cloud VM (CUDA GPU + Docker). 4. Automated deployment to local GPU — same easy install to local PC
(CUDA GPU + Docker).
:::

## Why not AI APIs (2/2)

::: {.lead .smaller-lead}
An AI provider I pay for, refusing to generate the satirical poster of the CEOs as zombies you saw before, and, after
I reminded it that satiric representation of public figures is protected free speech in USA, decided to serve me this
image instead
:::

::: {.provider-shots}
![](images/provider-lake.jpg){fig-alt="A calm mountain lake with a wooden pier: what the AI provider generated"}

![](images/provider-reply.jpg){fig-alt="The owner complains; the AI provider apologizes for a bizarre lecture about political satire followed by a picture of a mountain lake"}
:::

::: {.citation}
> Hustler Magazine, Inc. v. Falwell, 485 U.S. 46 (1988), is a landmark decision by the Supreme Court of the United
> States in which the Court held that parodies of public figures, even those intending to cause emotional distress,
> are protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the U.S. Constitution.

[— Wikipedia, "Hustler Magazine v. Falwell", CC BY-SA 4.0]{.credit}
:::

::: {.provider-caption}
**Not your weights, not your AI.**
:::

::: {.notes}
A hosted model decides what you may make; a local one does not — the case for local AI first. "Not your weights,
not your AI": even on a rented GPU, the open weights we run are ours; no provider can refuse a request or swap the
model. Its apology even
misnames the request.
:::
